title: Composite Shapes and Tessellations
seo_title: Grade 4 Composite Shapes and Tessellations Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Build composite 2-D shapes; draw and describe tessellated patterns; describe patterns in nature, everyday life and our cultural heritage (e.g. in buildings, beadwork, mats and cloth).
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 4 worksheets on composite shapes and tessellations: building shapes, counting shapes, which shapes tessellate and tessellated patterns. 100 questions with memos.
key_sub: Composite shapes are built from smaller shapes.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A composite shape is made of two or more shapes: a house shape is a square and a triangle.
  • Shapes tessellate when they cover a surface with no gaps and no overlaps, like floor tiles.
  • Squares, rectangles, triangles and regular hexagons tessellate. Circles do not.
  • Look for tessellations in nature (honeycomb) and in South African beadwork and wall art.

Examples

Example

Regular hexagons

3 meet at each point: 120° × 3 = 360°

Answer: they tessellate

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Only small shapesLook for bigger shapes made of smaller ones.
Circles tessellateCircles leave gaps.
Gaps or overlapsA tessellation has neither.

faq.q: What does CAPS Grade 4 say about transformations?
faq.a: Build composite 2-D shapes and tessellated patterns, and describe patterns in nature, everyday life and our cultural heritage.
A pattern of shapes that covers a surface with no gaps or overlaps.
Floors, walls, honeycomb and Ndebele designs.

items.q: Which two shapes make this house?
items.e: The walls are a square (4 equal sides) and the roof is a triangle (3 sides).

items.q: How many sides does the outline of the whole house have?
items.e: Go round the outside: 2 walls, the floor and 2 roof sides = 5 sides, so the outline is a pentagon. Do not add 4 + 3 = 7: the line where the roof meets the walls is inside.

items.q: Which two shapes make this arrow?
items.e: The long part is a rectangle and the point is a triangle.

items.q: Which two shapes make this tree?
items.e: The leaves are a triangle and the trunk is a thin rectangle.

items.q: How many triangles make this hexagon?
items.e: Count the triangles round the centre: 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and each side belongs to one triangle.

items.q: Which shapes make this hexagon?
items.e: The line cuts the hexagon into 2 pieces. Each piece has 4 sides and 1 pair of parallel sides, so each is a trapezium.

items.q: Which shapes make this trapezium?
items.e: Count the pieces: 3 triangles. Pattern blocks work like this: 3 triangles make 1 trapezium.

items.q: Which two shapes make this big triangle?
items.e: The top piece is a small triangle. The bottom piece has 4 sides and 1 pair of parallel sides: a trapezium.

items.q: Which shapes make this rectangle?
items.e: The line in the middle cuts the rectangle into 2 equal squares.

items.q: Which shapes make this square?
items.e: The line goes from one corner to the opposite corner. It cuts the square into 2 triangles.

items.q: Which shapes make this L shape?
items.e: A tall rectangle and a flat rectangle make the L. Neither piece has 4 equal sides, so they are not squares.

items.q: Which two shapes make this boat?
items.e: The sail is a triangle. The hull has 4 sides, with the top longer than the bottom: a trapezium.

items.q: Which shapes make this rocket?
items.e: The body is a rectangle. The nose is a triangle and there is a triangle fin on each side: 1 + 2 = 3 triangles.

items.q: A rectangle and 2 triangles make this shape. What is the name of the whole outline?
items.e: Go round the outside and count the sides: 6. So the outline is a hexagon.

items.q: A rectangle and a triangle make this shape. What is the name of the whole outline?
items.e: The sloping side of the triangle and the side of the rectangle go round the outside. The outline has 4 sides and 1 pair of parallel sides: a trapezium.

items.q: This rectangle is made from squares of the same size. How many squares?
items.e: There are 2 rows of 4 squares: 4 + 4 = 8. Adding the rows and columns (4 + 2 = 6) does not count the squares.

items.q: You join 2 squares of the same size along one side. Which shape do you make?
items.e: 2 squares side by side make a rectangle twice as long as it is wide. It has 4 sides, not 4 + 4 = 8.

items.q: Two right-angled triangles are the same. You join them along their longest sides. Which shape can you make?
items.e: Put the triangles together like the two halves of a sandwich cut corner to corner: they make a rectangle with 4 right angles.

items.q: Ayanda cuts a rectangle from one corner to the opposite corner. What two shapes does she get?
items.e: A cut from corner to corner makes 2 triangles. A cut across the middle would make 2 rectangles.

items.q: Which shape is made from a square and a triangle?
items.e: D is a square with a triangle on top. The others are a rectangle and a triangle, a trapezium and a triangle, and 2 triangles.

items.q: How many circles are in this robot?
items.e: 2 eyes and 2 buttons: 2 + 2 = 4 circles.

items.q: How many triangles are in this robot?
items.e: 1 on top of the head and 1 ear on each side: 1 + 2 = 3 triangles.

items.q: How many rectangles are in this robot? (A square is a rectangle too.)
items.e: Mouth, body, 2 arms and 2 legs are 6 rectangles. The square head is a rectangle too: 6 + 1 = 7.

items.q: How many shapes are in this robot altogether?
items.e: Count every shape: 3 triangles + 1 square + 6 rectangles + 4 circles = 14. Do not forget the eyes, mouth and buttons drawn on top of other shapes.

items.q: How many circles are in this train?
items.e: 2 wheels on the carriage and 3 wheels on the engine: 2 + 3 = 5 circles.

items.q: How many squares are in this train?
items.e: 2 square windows on the carriage and the square cabin on the engine: 2 + 1 = 3 squares.

items.q: How many rectangles are in this train? (A square is a rectangle too.)
items.e: 4 rectangles (carriage, engine, chimney, the join between them) and 3 squares, which are rectangles too: 4 + 3 = 7.

items.q: How many squares are in this picture?
items.e: The 2 windows are squares, and so are the walls of the house: 2 + 1 = 3 squares.

items.q: How many rectangles are in this picture? (A square is a rectangle too.)
items.e: The door and the tree trunk are rectangles (2). The 3 squares are rectangles too: 2 + 3 = 5.

items.q: How many shapes are in this picture altogether?
items.e: 3 squares + 2 rectangles + 2 triangles + 1 circle = 8 shapes.

items.q: How many triangles are in this boat?
items.e: 2 sails and the little flag at the top of the mast: 2 + 1 = 3 triangles.

items.q: What shape is the hull (the bottom part) of this boat?
items.e: The hull has 4 sides. The top and bottom are parallel but not the same length, so it is a trapezium.

items.q: How many triangles can you find in this picture?
items.e: There are 2 small triangles, and together they make 1 big triangle: 2 + 1 = 3.

items.q: How many triangles can you find in this picture?
items.e: 3 small triangles, 2 triangles made of 2 small ones next to each other, and 1 big one: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

items.q: How many triangles can you find in this picture?
items.e: 4 small triangles, and the big triangle made of all 4: 4 + 1 = 5.

items.q: How many triangles can you find in this square?
items.e: 4 small triangles meet in the middle. Each diagonal also cuts the square into 2 big triangles: 2 + 2 = 4 more. 4 + 4 = 8.

items.q: Neo counts the triangles in this picture and gets 4. What did he forget?
c: the big triangle made by all 4
items.e: There are 4 small triangles, but all 4 together make 1 big triangle too. 4 + 1 = 5.

items.q: How many rectangles can you find? (A square is a rectangle too.)
items.e: There are 2 squares, and they make 1 big rectangle together: 2 + 1 = 3.

items.q: How many rectangles can you find? (A square is a rectangle too.)
items.e: 3 small ones, 2 made of 2 small ones next to each other, and 1 big one: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

items.q: How many squares can you find?
items.e: 4 small squares, and the big square around all of them: 4 + 1 = 5.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: Every corner of B is the same number of squares from its matching corner of A, in the same direction, and B faces the same way. It was slid: a translation. Every corner moved 5 squares right and 4 squares up.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: Every corner of B is the same number of squares from its matching corner of A, in the same direction, and B faces the same way. It was slid: a translation. Every corner moved 5 squares right and 4 squares down.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is a mirror image of A: it faces the other way. Each corner of B is the same distance from the mirror line as its partner in A. It was flipped: a reflection. The mirror line is x = 5.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is a mirror image of A: it faces the other way. Each corner of B is the same distance from the mirror line as its partner in A. It was flipped: a reflection. The mirror line is y = 4: B is upside down but is not turned.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is a mirror image of A: it faces the other way. Each corner of B is the same distance from the mirror line as its partner in A. It was flipped: a reflection. The slanted side is on the left of A and on the right of B, at the same height.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. Point O does not move. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is A turned about the point O: it is not flipped (it is not a mirror image), and O does not move. It is a rotation. The side that pointed right from O now points down: a quarter turn clockwise.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. Point O does not move. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is A turned about the point O: it is not flipped (it is not a mirror image), and O does not move. It is a rotation. It is a half turn about O. It looks upside down, but a reflection in a horizontal line would not also swap left and right.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. Point O does not move. What happened to shape A?
items.e: B is A turned about the point O: it is not flipped (it is not a mirror image), and O does not move. It is a rotation. The bottom side pointed right from O and now points up: a quarter turn anticlockwise.

items.q: Shape A was moved to make shape B. What happened to shape A?
items.e: The sides of B are twice as long as the sides of A. A translation, reflection or rotation never changes the size, so B was enlarged. The bottom side of A is 3 squares long; the bottom side of B is 6 squares long.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape a reflection of the green shape?
items.e: In D the blue shape is reflected in a vertical line: it faces the other way, left to right. The others: A is turned a quarter turn clockwise; B is slid (a translation): it faces the same way; C is turned a half turn: upside down and back to front.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape a translation of the green shape?
items.e: In B the blue shape is slid (a translation): it faces the same way. The others: A is turned a half turn: upside down and back to front; C is reflected in a horizontal line: it is flipped upside down only; D is turned a quarter turn anticlockwise.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape a rotation of the green shape?
items.e: In A the blue shape is turned a quarter turn clockwise. The others: B is reflected in a vertical line: it faces the other way, left to right; C is reflected in a horizontal line: it is flipped upside down only; D is slid (a translation): it faces the same way.

items.q: In which picture is the blue shape the green shape reflected in a horizontal mirror line?
items.e: In C the blue shape is reflected in a horizontal line: it is flipped upside down only. The others: A is reflected in a vertical line: it faces the other way, left to right; B is turned a half turn: upside down and back to front; D is slid (a translation): it faces the same way.

items.q: The letter b is reflected in a vertical mirror line (flipped left to right). Which letter does it look like?
items.e: A vertical mirror flips left and right, so the round part moves to the other side of the stick but stays at the bottom: d.

items.q: The letter b is reflected in a horizontal mirror line (flipped upside down). Which letter does it look like?
items.e: A horizontal mirror flips top and bottom, so the stick now hangs down and the round part stays on the right: p.

items.q: The letter b is rotated a half turn. Which letter does it look like?
items.e: A half turn turns it upside down and back to front at the same time: the stick hangs down and the round part is on the left: q. This is not the same as a reflection.

items.q: A lift goes straight up from the ground floor to level 3. Which transformation is this?
items.e: The lift slides in one direction without turning or flipping, so it is a translation.

items.q: A door swings open on its hinges. Which transformation is this?
items.e: The door turns about a fixed line (the hinges). Seen from above, it turns about a point: a rotation.

items.q: Shape B is shape A turned a half turn. Ravi says, “B is upside down, so it must be a reflection.” What is wrong?
c: A half turn makes the shape smaller
Nothing: upside down always means a reflection
A reflection never turns a shape upside down
A half turn also turns a shape upside down
items.e: A half turn turns a shape upside down and back to front. A reflection makes a mirror image. Check: is B a mirror image of A, or is it A turned?

items.q: After a translation, a reflection or a rotation, which of these always stays the same?
items.e: These moves change where the shape is (and a reflection or rotation changes the way it faces), but never its size. The side lengths and angles always stay the same.

items.q: In this brick wall, how is each row placed compared with the row below it?
items.e: Each row is the row below slid half a brick sideways (and up one row). Nothing is flipped or turned, so it is a translation.

items.q: How many hexagons meet at the red dot?
items.e: 3 hexagons meet at each corner. Each angle is 120°, and 3 × 120° = 360°.

items.q: How many triangles meet at the red dot?
items.e: 6 triangles meet at each point. Each angle is 60°, and 6 × 60° = 360°.

items.q: Which two shapes make this floor tile pattern?
items.e: The large tiles have 8 equal sides (regular octagons) and the small tiles are squares turned on an angle. At each corner, 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.

items.q: How many tiles meet at the red dot?
items.e: 2 octagons and 1 square meet at each corner: 135° + 135° + 90° = 360°.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Every flag points the same way and is the same way up. Each one is the one before slid 1 tile to the right.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: The flags point right, left, right, left but stay the same way up: each is a mirror image of the one before, with the mirror line on the edge between the tiles. A half turn would also turn it upside down.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Each flag is upside down and points the other way. It is the one before turned a half turn about the middle of the edge between the tiles. A reflection flips it only one way.

items.q: This border pattern repeats one flag tile. How is each tile made from the tile before it?
items.e: Each flag is upside down but still points right. It is reflected in the line across the middle of the strip and then slid 1 tile along, like a trail of footprints.

items.q: Each tile is the tile before turned a quarter turn clockwise. Which tile comes next?
items.e: The flag on the pole points right, then down, then left. One more quarter turn clockwise makes it point up: D. The others: A: it is turned anticlockwise, back to the second tile; B: it is a mirror image of the right answer, flipped, not turned; C: it is turned one quarter turn too far, back to the start.

items.q: Each angle of a square is 90°. How many squares fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 90° = 4, so 4 squares fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°. How many equilateral triangles fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 60° = 6, so 6 equilateral triangles fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°. How many regular hexagons fit together around one point with no gaps?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 120° = 3, so 3 regular hexagons fit exactly around each point.

items.q: Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. Can regular pentagons fit around a point with no gaps?
items.e: 3 × 108° = 324°, which is less than 360°, so there is a gap of 36°. 4 × 108° = 432°, which is more than 360°, so a fourth pentagon would overlap. Regular pentagons do not tessellate.

items.q: Three regular pentagons meet at the red dot. Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. What is the size of the gap?
items.e: 3 × 108° = 324°. A full turn is 360°, so the gap is 360° − 324° = 36°. No regular shape has a 36° angle, so the gap cannot be filled with the same tiles.

items.q: Each angle of a regular octagon is 135°. Why do regular octagons not tessellate on their own?
items.e: Around a point the angles must add up to exactly 360°. 2 × 135° = 270° leaves a gap and 3 × 135° = 405° is too much. 135° does not divide exactly into 360°.

items.q: What does it mean when a shape tessellates?
c: It has at least one line of symmetry
It can be turned onto itself
Copies of it fit together with small gaps between them
Copies of it fit together with no gaps and no overlaps
items.e: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that covers a surface with no gaps and no overlaps, like the tiles on a floor.

items.q: Which shape tessellates on its own?
items.e: The regular hexagon (A): each angle is 120° and 3 × 120° = 360°. A regular pentagon (108°) and a regular octagon (135°) leave gaps, and circles cannot fit together without gaps.

items.q: Which shape does NOT tessellate on its own?
items.e: The regular pentagon (B): its angles are 108° and 360° ÷ 108° is not a whole number. Squares (4 × 90°), equilateral triangles (6 × 60°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°) all fit exactly around a point.

items.q: Why do circles not tessellate?
c: They have no angles, so they fit anywhere
Their curved edges always leave gaps
items.e: When circles touch, there are always curved gaps between them. A tessellation can have no gaps.

sets.title: Patterns in nature and everyday life

c: a cylinder and a square-based pyramid
items.e: The tall part has 2 circle ends and a curved side: a cylinder. The roof has a circle base and a point: a cone. Rectangles and triangles are flat 2-D shapes.

c: a square-based pyramid and a sphere
items.e: The scoop is round like a ball: a sphere. The cone comes to a point and has a circle at the top: a cone.

items.q: This model house is made of two objects. Which two?
c: a rectangular prism and a square-based pyramid
a rectangular prism and a triangular prism
items.e: The bottom has 6 rectangle faces: a rectangular prism. The roof has a triangle at each end and does not come to a point: a triangular prism.

items.q: This tower is made of two objects. Which two?
c: a cube and a square-based pyramid
a cube and a triangular prism
items.e: The bottom has 6 square faces: a cube. The top has 4 triangle faces that meet at a point: a square-based pyramid. A cone has a circle base.

c: a triangular prism and a cone
items.e: The long part is a cylinder and the tip is a cone. A rectangle and a triangle are only the flat outline.

items.q: This tent is shaped like which object?
items.e: It has a triangle at each end joined by rectangles, and it does not come to a point: a triangular prism.

items.q: How many faces does this tent have? Count the floor too.
items.e: You can see only 2 faces. A tent has 2 triangle ends and 3 rectangles (2 sloping sides and the floor): 2 + 3 = 5.

items.q: This is a solid stack of cubes with no gaps. How many cubes are in it?
items.e: Each layer has 2 × 2 = 4 cubes and there are 2 layers: 4 + 4 = 8. You can see only 7 of them; the other 1 is hidden behind the others.

items.q: This is a solid stack of cubes with no gaps. How many cubes are in it?
items.e: Each layer has 3 × 2 = 6 cubes and there are 2 layers: 6 + 6 = 12. You can see only 10 of them; the other 2 are hidden behind the others.

items.q: This is a solid stack of cubes with no gaps. How many cubes are in it?
items.e: Each layer has 3 × 3 = 9 cubes and there are 2 layers: 9 + 9 = 18. You can see only 14 of them; the other 4 are hidden behind the others.

items.q: Chloe is tiling a bathroom floor that is 2 m long and 1,5 m wide with square tiles 50 cm long. How many tiles are needed?
items.e: Change metres to centimetres: 200 cm and 150 cm. 200 ÷ 50 = 4 tiles along and 150 ÷ 50 = 3 tiles across. 4 × 3 = 12 tiles. (4 + 3 = 7 adds instead of multiplying.)

items.q: A kitchen splashback is 120 cm long and 60 cm high. It is covered with square tiles 20 cm long. How many tiles are needed?
items.e: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 tiles along and 60 ÷ 20 = 3 tiles up. 6 × 3 = 18 tiles. (6 is only one row.)

items.q: A classroom floor is 8 m long and 6 m wide. Carpet tiles are squares 50 cm long. How many carpet tiles cover the floor?
items.e: 50 cm is half a metre, so 2 tiles fit in each metre. 8 m = 16 tiles along and 6 m = 12 tiles across. 16 × 12 = 192 tiles. (48 is the area in square metres, not the number of tiles.)

items.q: A border of tiles 15 cm long runs along a wall 3 m long. How many tiles are in the border?
Floor tiles come in boxes of 12. A tiler needs 100 tiles. How many boxes must be bought?
items.e: 100 ÷ 12 = 8 remainder 4. 8 boxes hold only 96 tiles, so a 9th box is needed for the last 4 tiles.

items.q: A tile pattern has a square, a regular hexagon and a regular dodecagon at every corner. The square’s angle is 90° and the hexagon’s angle is 120°. What is the angle of the dodecagon?
items.e: The angles around a point add up to 360°. 360° − 90° − 120° = 150°. (270° and 240° take away only one of the angles; 210° uses 60° for the hexagon.)

items.q: In a geometry app, Precious reflects the point (2, 3) in the line x = 5, then translates it 2 squares up. Where does it end up?
items.e: (2, 3) is 3 squares left of x = 5, so its image is 3 squares right: (8, 3). Then 2 up: (8, 5).

items.q: Sarah designs a logo in a drawing program. The point (7, 4) is rotated a half turn about (5, 4). Where does it go?
items.e: (7, 4) is 2 squares right of (5, 4). A half turn turns right into left, so the image is 2 squares left: (3, 4). (5, 6) and (5, 2) are quarter turns; (1, 4) is too far.

items.q: A stamp makes a pattern along a strip. The first print is at x = 1, and each new print is translated 4 squares right. What is the x-coordinate of the 6th print?
items.e: From the 1st print to the 6th print there are 5 moves: 1 + 5 × 4 = 21. (25 counts 6 moves.)

items.q: Nomsa wants to tile a floor with regular pentagons only. What will happen?
c: The tiles will fit if there is an even number
There will be gaps between the tiles
The tiles will fit with no gaps
The tiles will fit if they are made smaller
items.e: Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°. 3 × 108° = 324° leaves a 36° gap at every corner. Making the tiles smaller does not change the angles.
